title: The Lighthouse Keeper's Wife
teaser: Every night for forty years, she has climbed the tower to light the lamp. Every night, something climbs behind her.
body: Mara Voss had kept the light at Coldharbor Point for forty-one years, ever since her husband Elias drowned in the strait during the storm of '84. The fishermen said she'd gone strange after that — climbing the tower every night at dusk, muttering to herself on the stairs, refusing to let anyone else near the lamp room. They didn't know the truth. They didn't know that Elias never really left.

He came back the winter after his death, soaked and grey and smiling with a mouth that hung slightly too wide. He didn't speak. He only followed her up the spiral stairs each evening, three steps behind, his wet boots leaving no prints on the stone.

At first she'd screamed. She'd thrown a lantern at him, watched it pass through his chest and shatter against the wall. But screaming did nothing, and the tower was a long way from town, and eventually you learn to live with the thing that loves you even after it has stopped being alive.

"Just to the top, Elias," she would say, the way she once spoke to him when he was a boy learning the stairs himself, before they were married, before the sea took him. "Just to the top, and then you can rest."

He never rested. He waited at the bottom of the stairs every dusk, patient as driftwood, and climbed behind her, and at the top he would stand in the doorway of the lamp room and watch her light the wick, and something like joy would cross his ruined face, and then he would be gone until the next evening.
She told herself this was a kind of marriage. Two people, keeping a light burning for the ships that passed in the dark. It didn't matter that one of them was dead. Devotion didn't require breath.
But in the autumn of her sixty-third year, something changed.

She noticed it first as a smell — brine and rot, thicker than before, curling up the stairwell ahead of her rather than trailing behind. She noticed that the wet footprints, faint as they were, no longer stopped at the lamp room door. They circled the base of the lens. They pressed themselves into the corners where the light didn't reach.
And she noticed that Elias's smile, when she turned to check on him, had begun to show teeth that were not his own.
"You're not climbing behind me anymore," she said one evening, halfway up the two hundred and twelve steps, her lamp throwing her shadow long against the curved wall. "You're climbing beside me."

The thing that wore her husband's face did not answer. It never had. But its head tilted, slow and wrong, like a marionette finding a new joint, and for the first time in forty years she understood that grief is a door, and doors can be walked through from either side.
She kept climbing. What else was there to do? The light needed lighting. The ships needed warning off the rocks. Duty was the only rope she had left to hold, and she gripped it with both hands.

At the top, she turned the crank that woke the great lens, and the beam swept out over the black water, and for one moment — one single, suspended moment — she saw the thing beside her clearly, fully, in a way she had spent four decades refusing to see. It was not Elias. It had never been Elias. It was something that had found Elias in the water the night he drowned, and had liked the shape of him, and had worn that shape up her stairs every night since because it had discovered, long ago, that grief will let almost anything in if it only wears a familiar face.
"Get out," she whispered.
It smiled wider. Somewhere below, deep in the tower's throat, she heard the sea-slick sound of something else beginning to climb.

She realized, with the particular calm of a woman who has spent half her life expecting this exact moment, that she had never been keeping one visitor at bay. She had been holding a door open for years, telling herself it was love, while more of them gathered in the dark beneath the stairs, waiting for her strength to finally give out.

The lamp turned above her, patient and enormous, throwing its warning across the water for ships she would never meet, sailors she would never save from rocks they didn't know were there. She understood, finally, that the light had never been for them.
It was the only thing standing between her and the stairs.
She reached out and touched the thing wearing her husband's face, and for the first time in forty-one years, her hand did not pass through him.
His skin was cold as harbor water, and real, and reaching back.
Below, the footsteps kept climbing.

She did not run. There was nowhere in Coldharbor Point that stairs did not lead down into the dark, and nowhere the dark did not know her name by now. So she simply turned the crank one final notch, brightening the beam until it burned white across the strait, and she said, gently, the way you'd speak to a child who has been lost a very long time —
"Alright, then. Come up."

The light kept turning long after there was no one left to wind it. Sailors passing Coldharbor Point still speak of the beam, steady and searching, sweeping the black water every night without fail — and of the second shadow they sometimes see moving in the lamp room window, patient, keeping time with the first.
